name: Arsenic face enameling

lead: Face enameling was a Victorian-to-early-1900s practice of applying thick opaque white paint to produce a flawless porcelain look and to hide wrinkles and blemishes.
Historical accounts associate such cosmetics with lead and arsenic compounds. Arsenic was also sold in soaps and in eaten complexion wafers promoted for clearing skin.

paras: Historical accounts describe layered opaque paint applied by a practitioner. This article does not describe methods.

Arsenic exposure can cause scabbing, blistering, sores, hair loss and, with prolonged exposure, organ failure. Lead was classified as a poison in the UK in 1631 and was largely replaced by pearl white and talc by the early 1900s.

chain: Opaque white coating applied to face
angle.text: The coating gave an even, pale surface that hid lines and marks. Arsenic and lead ingredients are documented as poisonous.

lead: Face enameling refers to historical cosmetic coatings meant to give a pale, porcelain-like face. It sits within a long history of whitening make-up using lead and arsenic [1].

Wikipedia records Elizabethan make-up of vinegar, chalk and arsenic to whiten skin and soften creases, and arsenic complexion wafers advertised in late 19th-century newspapers to clear blemishes [2]. The Science Museum Group notes that Dr Campbell's arsenical wafers and Dr Mackenzie's arsenic soap continued to be sold into the 20th century [1].

paras: White lead make-up such as Venetian ceruse was used for centuries and is associated with Queen Elizabeth I's pale complexion; lead was classified as a UK poison in 1631 [1]. Arsenic appeared in washes, hair dyes and tooth cement listed in an 1866 book, and orpiment in a 1776 depilatory recipe [1].

The Science Museum Group notes arsenic exposure can cause scabbing, blistering and sores, and prolonged exposure organ failure [1]. Wikipedia states that some arsenic was inevitably absorbed into the bloodstream from cosmetics [2].

timeline.event: Lead is classified as a poison in the UK [1].
Arnold J Cooley's book lists arsenic in cosmetic washes, nail treatments and hair dyes [1].
Arsenic complexion wafers advertised in US newspapers [2].
